Learning Objectives
Review the basic principles of general anesthesia, the main classes of anesthetic agents, and
the manner in which general anesthesia differs from other types of anesthesia, such as
monitored anesthesia care.
Compare general anesthesia and regional anesthesia, particularly with regard to orthopaedic
procedures.
List safety concerns associated with and complications that may arise from general anesthesia,
including patient positioning–associated nerve injuries.
Discuss the evaluation of a patient ready to undergo anesthesia and list aspects of the medical
history that are pertinent to the preoperative assessment.
Outline the detailed steps and sequence of events for general anesthesia, starting with
induction.

Basic Principles of General Anesthesia
Goals
Pharmacologically induced, reversible loss of consciousness, without ability to feel pain and
with abatement of all reflexes (including airway reflexes)

Goals
General anesthesia is a pharmacologically induced, reversible loss of consciousness,
without ability to feel pain and with abatement of all reflexes (including airway
reflexes).1-4 This is different from conscious sedation and monitored anesthesia care
because of the need for airway manipulation secondary to potentially inadequate
patient ventilation given the depth of anesthesia. General anesthesia involves airway
manipulation with the use of an endotracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway (LMA), or
supraglottic airway device.
Modes of Delivery
Five classes of anesthetic agents: intravenous anesthetic agents, inhalational anesthetic
agents, intravenous sedatives, synthetic opioids, neuromuscular-blocking agents1-4

Modes of Delivery
Five classes of anesthetic agents exist. These include intravenous anesthetic agents,
inhalational anesthetic agents, intravenous sedatives, synthetic opioids, and
neuromuscular-blocking agents.1-4 These provide the essential components of
anesthesia: amnesia, anxiolysis, analgesia, and akinesia. Usually, delivery of general
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:17 PM
AAOS | General Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004007
2/31

anesthesia involves a mixture of intravenous anesthetic agents (induction) and
inhalational anesthetic agents (maintenance). Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) is
general anesthesia via only intravenous agents rather than volatile anesthetic gas. TIVA
is considered ideal in patients who are predisposed to postoperative nausea/vomiting,
which often is caused by inhalational gas.3 may also TIVA be used in situations involving
evoked potential monitoring.
Indications
Procedures requiring deep relaxation for long periods of time
Failure of local or regional anesthesia
Expected hemodynamic instability or surgical complications
Uncooperative patients (dementia, pediatrics)
Patient contraindications to regional or local anesthesia ( ie, need for protected airway)
Procedures requiring certain patient positioning, such that airway protection will be a safer
option ( ie, prone or lateral patient positioning, bed turned away from the anesthesiologist,
drapes covering the face without easy access to the airway)
Complicating Patient Factors
Difficult airway
Considerable comorbidities (ie, aortic stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, or heart failure)
In these patients, airway manipulation and physiologic changes associated with general
anesthesia may increase the risk of morbidity; alternative approaches such as regional
anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care may be safer options.1-4
Necessary Equipment
Ventilator, gas supply, vaporizers, flow meters, breathing circuits, and suction canisters
Mandatory American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) monitors must be used, including
electrocardiography, blood pressure, blood oxygen saturation, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and
temperature monitors.1
Basic airway accessories: face mask, laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, stylets, oral and nasal
areas, LMAs

General Anesthesia Versus Regional Anesthesia
Many procedures, particularly orthopaedic procedures, can be performed via general
anesthesia or regional anesthesia, which includes neuraxial techniques and/or peripheral
nerve blocks.5-7
General anesthesia requires the use of multiple intravenous or inhalational anesthetic agents
to achieve a deep plane of unconsciousness.
Conversely, regional anesthesia involves localized placement of anesthetic to numb the
surgical site, often sparing systemic opioids and other agents; sedation, although unnecessary,
often is administered in addition to regional anesthesia so patients are not aware of the sights
and sounds of the surgical procedure.

General Anesthesia Versus Regional Anesthesia
Considerable controversy exists with regard to the potential effect of the type of
anesthesia (general anesthesia versus regional anesthesia) on patient-associated
recovery outcomes, such as hospital length of stay, narcotic use, pain, and delirium,
particularly in older individuals. Because total hip and total knee arthroplasty are
suitable for neuraxial techniques and the growing prevalence of these procedures is
increasingly affecting national healthcare costs, these procedures are at the forefront of
this debate.5,6
Therefore, comparisons of total hip and total knee arthroplasty under general
anesthesia versus regional anesthesia have been studied extensively. The use of
neuraxial anesthesia for total hip or total knee arthroplasty has been shown to be
independently associated with improved outcomes, including lower systemic
complications (pulmonary embolism, cardiac complications infections, 30-day mortality,
etc.) compared with general anesthesia for the same procedures.5,6 These findings have
been confirmed in other studies, which also have found similarly decreased mortality
rates and reduced risk of thromboembolism, surgical time, and blood loss in patients
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:17 PM
AAOS | General Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004007
4/31

who underwent neuraxial anesthesia versus general anesthesia for the same
procedures.7 In addition, a patient’s tolerable blood pressure with hypotensive
epidural/spinal anesthesia appears to be much lower than an acceptable blood pressure
with general anesthesia; the explanation for this has not yet been determined. Possible
mechanisms include patient selection and procedure type. Alternatively, physiologic
explanations include improved perfusion at the tissue level under the sympathectomy of
a neuraxial block and the effect of volatile agents on decreasing cardiac contractility.
Although several of these studies have been criticized for their small sample sizes and
biased sample populations, a movement exists toward greater use of regional
anesthesia as an alternative to general anesthesia for procedures in which regional
techniques can be used;5 however, because general anesthesia is quite safe, particularly
in healthy patients without comorbidities, the decision to perform a procedure under
general anesthesia versus regional anesthesia ultimately is based on patient discretion
and anesthesiologist comfort with regional techniques (Resource 1).
Adverse Effects and Complications of General Anesthesia
General anesthesia is very safe. Rates of death from general anesthesia are estimated to be
approximately 1 in every 150,000 individuals; however, general anesthesia is associated with
common adverse effects and more rare, serious complications.
Common Postoperative Adverse Effects
Confusion or memory loss, particularly in elderly patients1-4
Urinary retention1-4
Postoperative nausea/vomiting, particularly in younger female patients and/or patients with a
history of motion sickness or previous postoperative nausea/vomiting, usually triggered by
inhalational gas1-4
Sore throat from endotracheal tube or LMA1-4
Patients who are sicker and undergoing lengthy procedures have an increased risk for more
serious complications, such as persistent confusion, heart attack, pneumonia, embolism, or
stroke.1-4

Rare Complications
Malignant hyperthermia and pseudocholinesterase deficiency are genetic conditions that
require advanced planning to minimize patient morbidity and mortality if general anesthesia is
required.8-11

Rare Complications
Malignant hyperthermia is a rare, inherited, potentially lethal syndrome characterized by
hypermetabolic activity, marked carbon dioxide production, altered skeletal muscle tone,
metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalemia. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile
inhalational anesthetic agents and succinylcholine. Clinical manifestations include
muscle rigidity, rhabdomyolysis, high temperatures, acidosis, organ failure, and possibly
death. Primary treatment of malignant hyperthermia consists of dantrolene (calcium
channel blocker); active cooling may be required. Diagnosis is made via muscle biopsy.
Specific malignant hyperthermia–related processing is available only at select sites in the
united states.8-10
Pseudocholinesterase deficiency is a rare, autosomal recessive blood plasma enzyme
abnormality in which the production of butyrylcholinesterase (also
pseudocholinesterase) is impaired. Individuals with this abnormality are sensitive to
certain anesthetic drugs, including the muscle relaxants succinylcholine and mivacurium
and ester local anesthetic agents that are metabolized by butyrylcholinesterase.
Alternative agents should be used in these individuals.11
Preoperative Planning
Risk identification is the foundation of preoperative evaluation.
The ASA physical status classification system is essential in classifying a patient’s state of
health.
A thorough preoperative evaluation depends on a combination of the patient history, physical
examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies.

Preoperative Planning
Risk identification is the foundation of preoperative evaluation. The ASA physical status
classification system is essential in classifying a patient’s state of health (Table 1). The
ASA physical status classification system provides uniform classification of a patient’s
preoperative state of health but does not predict perioperative risk.12,13 Other aspects
of the preoperative evaluation include a patient history and a physical examination
involving an airway examination, with or without laboratory tests; electrocardiography;
chest radiography; and other evaluations, such as pulmonary function tests or cardiac
tests, if relevant.2,3 Signs and symptoms of instability or insufficient management of
identified medical conditions and risks require additional investigation and optimization.
The anesthesiologist and the surgeon must communicate directly to coordinate and
optimize preoperative planning and surgical management.

Importance of Patient Positioning
Careful attention to patient positioning during general anesthesia is essential because patients
are unaware of any positioning-induced pain they may have that may lead to potential
postoperative injury.14-23
In addition, certain patient positions influence cardiorespiratory function, resulting in altered
hemodynamic and cardiorespiratory characteristics.
Additional important aspects about patient positioning during general anesthesia:
Surgical positions include supine, prone, Trendelenburg, reverse Trendelenburg, lithotomy,
sitting (beach-chair), or lateral decubitus positions.
Patient positioning is the responsibility of the surgical and anesthesiology teams.

Priority must be directed toward the airway in planning for surgical positioning and during
the process of active patient positioning.
All pressure points must be vigilantly identified, padded, and protected.
Positioning-Related Musculoskeletal and Peripheral Nerve/Plexus Nerve
Injury
Perioperative peripheral nerve injuries continue to cause patient disability, leading to multiple
malpractice claims each year. Of the 11,000 claims filed between 2005 and 2014, 21% were
related to nerve injury.20

Positioning-Related Musculoskeletal and Peripheral Nerve/Plexus
Nerve Injury
Certain patient characteristics have been reported to be associated with perioperative
neuropathy. Although the literature is insufficient and the exact mechanisms are
unclear, observational studies have reported an association between preoperative
patient conditions (ie, obesity, diabetes mellitus, vascular disease, age, and low body
mass index) and upper and lower extremity neuropathies. Descriptive observational
studies report brachial and ulnar neuropathies in patients with specific preexisting
conditions, such as diabetes mellitus, vascular disease, alcoholism, male sex, and
extremes of body weight. Case reports indicate that upper and lower extremity
neuropathies occur in patients with diabetes mellitus, preexisting paresthesias, heavy
alcohol use, and smoking history.20
To minimize risk of upper extremity injury, efforts should be made to minimize pressure
on the ulnar nerve by tucking the patient's arms by the side in a thumbs-up position. If
abduction or flexion is necessary, it should be less than 90°. If head rotation is required,
contralateral arm abduction should be avoided because of the risk of brachial plexus
injury. Arms may be tucked at the side of the patient to avoid excess traction.20,21

9/3/26, 4:17 PM

Overall, proper communication between nursing, anesthesia, and surgery teams and
frequent patient positioning checks can help reduce the incidence of perioperative
injuries.
Positioning-Related Upper Extremity Injuries
In the upper extremity, ulnar nerve injury is most common, estimated to account for
approximately 28% of acute perioperative nerve injuries, followed by brachial plexus (28%),
radial (3%), and median (4%) nerve injuries.14-20
Ulnar nerve (C7, C8-T1): often injured in the supine position with the arms incorrectly secured
to armrests or in the lateral decubitus position with hyperextended shoulders; injury is
characterized by a tingling sensation or numbness along the little finger and weakness of
abduction and/or adduction of the fingers. Physical examination of the hand reveals
hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the distal and the proximal
interphalangeal joints of the ring and the little fingers (ulnar claw).14-20
Radial nerve (C5-T1): involves wrist drop and numbness along the posterior surface of the
lower part of the arm, the posterior surface of the forearm, and a variable small area on the
dorsum of the hand and the lateral three-and-one-half fingers19,20
Median nerve (C5-T1)—Several studies have reported median nerve injury after prolonged use
of an automated blood pressure cuff.21 This injury results in paresthesia along the palmar
aspect of the lateral fingers. Motor manifestations include weakness of abduction and
opposition of the thumb, weak wrist flexion, and the forearm maintained in supination. The
muscles of the thenar eminence become wasted, and the hand appears flattened.
Positioning-Related Lower Extremity Injuries
Nerves of the lower extremity, including the sciatic nerve, common peroneal nerve, femoral
nerve, obturator nerve, and saphenous nerve, have been observed to manifest perioperative
injury after prolonged lithotomy position.20
Positioning-Induced Changes in Cardiorespiratory Mechanics
Supine position: reduced functional residual capacity secondary to cephalad displacement of
the diaphragm
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:17 PM
AAOS | General Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004007
13/31

Trendelenburg position: accentuated cephalad displacement of the diaphragm; although
occasionally used to increase venous return to the heart to improve cardiac output, it may
reduce cardiac output secondary to the abdominal viscera resting against the heart; increased
intracranial pressure.
Prone position: cephalad displacement of the diaphragm with restricted caudad expansion,
resulting in increased peak airway pressures; compression of inferior vena cava and aorta;
turning the patient’s head may restrict vertebral artery flow and venous drainage.
Patients undergoing spine surgery in the prone position are at risk for unilateral or bilateral
blindness secondary to posterior ischemic optic neuropathy.23
Although prolonged direct compression of the globe may cause blindness, it is not the usual
cause. Several case reports and series have investigated perioperative visual complications
after spinal surgery in the prone position; factors believed to be associated with this
occurrence are large blood loss, long surgical duration in the prone position, massive
transfusion, extreme prolonged hypotension, and preoperative anemia.24
Therefore, studies show that factors intrinsic to the patient (ie, ocular vascular anatomy,
coexisting illnesses) or to the surgical procedure (ie, positioning on frames, type and amount
of fluid and blood replacement) may contribute to postoperative visual deficits.24,25 Although
surgeons are unsure of methods to prevent this complication, surgeons should be aware of
these factors and ensure the head is not substantially below the heart to avoid increased
ophthalmologic venous pressure during prone patient positioning, which may help reduce
risks.
Lateral decubitus position: compression of the inferior vena cava; dependent lung is
underventilated but has increased blood flow, whereas the independent lung is overventilated
but has reduced blood flow, which may result in hypoxemia because of ventilation to
perfusion mismatch; depends on axillary neurovascular compression.
Sitting (beach-chair) position—Venous pressure differential between the right atrium and
exposed veins higher than the heart (located at a surgical site, such as shoulder or brain) may
result in venous air embolism. Sitting position also may result in reduced cardiac output and,
therefore, lower cerebral perfusion pressure; hypotensive bradycardic events may be
associated with shoulder arthroscopy in the beach-chair position, thought to occur secondary
to the same mechanisms underlying vasovagal syncope, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, and
orthostatic hypotension.26,27
Lithotomy position: cephalad displacement of the diaphragm; inferior vena cava obstruction
with cephalad abdominal compression.

Monitors in General Anesthesia
Standard ASA monitors1-4
Continuous electrocardiography
Noninvasive arterial blood pressure (at least every 5 minutes)
Continuous pulse oximetry
Oxygen analyzer with a low oxygen concentration limit alarm
Capnography (end-tidal carbon dioxide)
Temperature
Additional monitors
Invasive continuous arterial blood pressure
Central venous pressure: surrogate of intravascular volume/preload in the absence of left
ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, or mitral valve disease
Pulmonary arterial/capillary wedge pressure: monitors cardiac filling pressures, cardiac
output, derived hemodynamic parameters, mixed venous oxygen saturation
Peripheral nerve stimulators: monitors neuromuscular function
Somatosensory-evoked potentials, motor-evoked potentials: monitors neurologic injury
Electroencephalography: monitors cerebral ischemia
Cerebral oximetry: monitors cerebral oxygenation; measures oxygenation of blood within the
first few millimeters of the frontal cortex
Bispectral index: uses electroencephalographic signals to measure the depth of
consciousness and sedation: 100, awake; 60 to 90, sedated; 40 to 60, general anesthesia; 0,
coma.
Stages of Anesthesia
Stage 1, induction: time from awake state to unconscious state with amnesia and analgesia
Stage 2, delirium/excitement: begins with loss of consciousness, characterized by irregular and
unpredictable respiratory and heart rate, breath holding, reflex activity (including non-
purposeful muscle movements), vomiting, laryngospasm, and arrhythmias
Stage 3, surgical anesthesia: characterized by achievement of minimum alveolar
concentration, loss of reflex activity (including laryngeal reflexes), muscle relaxation, and
shallow regular breathing
Stage 4, overdose: cardiorespiratory collapse

General Anesthesia Sequence of Events
Induction
Standard induction of general anesthesia begins with loss of consciousness via inhalational
and/or intravenous administration of anesthetic agents.1-4
After loss of consciousness, before the administration of paralytic agents in a non-
spontaneously breathing patient, the ability to ventilate with the use of a mask is evaluated.
If endotracheal intubation will be performed, paralytic agents often are administered (not
always required) to promote vocal cord paralysis to facilitate easy intubation.
Rapid Sequence Induction
An alternative to the standard method of induction of general anesthesia in which an
intravenous induction agent is followed immediately by succinylcholine (paralytic agent) and
subsequent direct laryngoscopy with intubation, omitting any mask ventilation1-4

Rapid Sequence Induction
Rapid sequence induction frequently is used in patients with aspiration risk, such as
those with a full stomach, gastroparesis, small bowel obstruction, or pregnancy.
Pressure applied externally to the cricoid cartilage from the time of induction until the
endotracheal tube is secured between the cords with the cuff inflated is intended to
compress the esophagus and reduce the risk of gastric fluids refluxing into the pharynx
and trachea; however, evidence for this is controversial.4
Airway Placement
Two types of airways may be after following induction of general anesthesia: an LMA or an
endotracheal tube.

Airway Placement

An LMA is not a secure airway because it does not isolate the lungs from potential
aspiration; therefore, it should be avoided in patients at risk for aspiration (Figure 1). A
supraglottic airway also is an important treatment option in the difficult airway
algorithm; if endotracheal intubation cannot be achieved easily, a supraglottic airway can
be used as a rescue device in the difficult airway algorithm (Figure 2). An LMA is sized
based on patient weight.28

Endotracheal tube intubation is achieved via direct laryngoscopy (blade), videoscope, or
fiberoptic scope. Fiberoptic scopes also can be used to aid in visualization for difficult
airways; they can be used in awake, lightly sedated patients or after the induction of
general anesthesia if the anesthesiologist is confident the patient can be ventilated after
potential loss of spontaneous respiration. Endotracheal tube sizes 7.0 and 8.0 are
standard for uncomplicated adult female and male airways, respectively.4

Anesthetic Agents
Propofol is the primary anesthetic agent that results in unconsciousness, acting rapidly
for induction and maintenance of anesthesia. It also has antiemetic properties. Ketamine
is a dissociative anesthetic agent that also has analgesic effects. Because of its
dissociative properties, ketamine may result in hallucinations and, therefore, often is
administered in combination with benzodiazepines to prevent hallucinations. In
addition, ketamine is a sialagogue, resulting in increased secretions, and often is
administered in combination with an anticholinergic agent, such as glycopyrrolate, to
decrease risk of laryngospasm. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that has
sedative, sympatholytic, and analgesic properties; it also preserves respiratory drive.
Inhalational Anesthetic Agents
Inhalational anesthetics are liquids transformed by vaporization into gas for rapid absorption
into and elimination via pulmonary circulation.
Their concentration in the brain and effect on the depth of anesthesia is directly related to
concentration absorbed in the alveoli.
Depth of anesthesia is determined based on measurement of minimal alveolar concentration,
which is defined as the concentration that will prevent movement in 50% of patients in
response to a painful stimulus (surgical incision).
Inhalational agents decrease cardiac contractility and cause hypotension.

Inhalational Anesthetic Agents
Sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane are volatile halogenated agents. Because of its
noxious smell, desflurane may cause coughing or laryngospasm on induction of general
anesthesia. These agents may severely depress ventilatory response. Halogenated
volatile anesthetic agents are triggers of malignant hyperthermia and must be avoided in
patients with a personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia because of the high
risk of morbidity and mortality associated with this condition. Nitrous oxide is an
odorless, non-halogenated agent. Because its minimal alveolar concentration is very high

Inhalational Agents on Evoked Potentials
Volatile agents interfere with sensory and motor-evoked potentials and should be used
sparingly if monitoring somatosensory-evoked potentials or avoided altogether if monitoring
motor-evoked potentials.

Inhalational Agents on Evoked Potentials
Inhalational agents substantially affect somatosensory- and motor-evoked potentials,
which are commonly monitored intraoperatively in spine procedures to evaluate the
integrity of ascending sensory tracts and descending motor pathways, respectively.
Compromise of a neurologic pathway is evident with a 10% increase in the latency
and/or a 50% decrease in the amplitude of evoked potential waveforms. Although all
anesthetic agents influence these waveforms to some degree, volatile anesthetic agents
most substantially interfere with signaling, causing increased cortical latency and
decreased cortical amplitude, which may be confused with neurologic injury (Table 3).
Desflurane and sevoflurane are more forgiving with somatosensory-evoked potentials
than agents such as enflurane and isoflurane. Nitrous oxide should be avoided
completely during monitoring because it has profound depressant effects on
somatosensory- and visual-evoked potentials if combined with a volatile agent. With
regard to somatosensory-evoked potentials, volatile agents result in a dose-dependent
decrease in amplitude and increase in latency; therefore, levels of volatile anesthetic
agent should not exceed a minimal alveolar concentration of 1.0. Motor-evoked
potentials are exquisitely sensitive to inhalational agents. Therefore, volatile agents
should be avoided during recording of motor-evoked potentials in favor of TIVA30 (Table
3).

Intravenous Sedatives
Benzodiazepines often are administered as premedication for general anesthesia.
Midazolam is the most common benzodiazepine administered preoperatively and provides
anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia.

Intravenous Sedatives
Benzodiazepines often are administered as premedication for general anesthesia
because they provide anxiolysis and amnesia. The most common preoperative
benzodiazepine is midazolam. Other agents include diazepam and lorazepam, which are
longer acting agents compared to midazolam. All benzodiazepines suppress respiratory
drive in response to hypercarbia and, therefore, should be administered cautiously in
patients with elevated baseline carbon dioxide, such as in patients with chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease.
Synthetic Opioids
Opioids are used for analgesia and during the induction of general anesthesia to blunt
sympathetic response to endotracheal intubation.

In addition to causing considerable respiratory depression, opioids cause miosis,
bradycardia, constipation, urinary retention, and chest wall rigidity. Synthetic opioids,
including alfentanil, sufentanil, remifentanil, and fentanyl, produce rapid and intense
analgesia. Fentanyl and sufentanil are 100 and 1,000 times more potent than morphine,
respectively. Remifentanil is a short-acting opioid that is quick to be metabolized and
results in no residual analgesia; however, tolerance may occur, resulting in increased
opioid requirement postoperatively (opioid-induced hyperalgesia).3,4
Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs
Neuromuscular-blocking agents cause full-body muscle relaxation or paralysis, including loss
of gag reflexes.
These are not necessary for general anesthesia but often facilitate intubation by opening vocal
cords and are particularly useful in orthopaedic procedures or for large abdominal procedures
in which muscle relaxation is desired.

Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs
Neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs) are categorized as competitive (non-
depolarizing) or non-competitive (depolarizing) agents. Succinylcholine is a
noncompetitive, short-acting NMBD with an onset action of 1 minute and a duration of
action of less than 10 minutes. After binding to the receptor site, it mimics acetylcholine
and causes muscular fasciculations. Therefore, it makes succinylcholine a commonly
used agent in rapid sequence intubations or for laryngospasm; however, it may trigger
malignant hyperthermia in patients with a personal or family history of this condition.
Atracurium, cisatracurium, pancuronium, vecuronium, and rocuronium are competitive
NMBDs that are slower acting agents compared with succinylcholine, with an action
onset of 1 to 3 minutes and a duration of action of approximately 30 to 40 minutes.
These agents usually are used during maintenance of anesthesia to maintain muscle
relaxation.
